doc.title: Randy Sandke interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997

title: Stanley Crouch, Lincoln Center and Benny Goodman's reputation
summary: He doubts Lincoln Center's canon is racially neutral and defends Goodman as a color-barrier breaker; earlier greats succeeded despite segregation.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: there, as much as they deny it. And I’ve sat down and I’ve talked to Stanley Crouch, I know Stanley Crouch, I know Wynton Marsalis a little bit, I mean we’ve talked a couple of times. I think I’ve talked more in depth with Stanley Crouch. And like he says that it’s not a racial thing, like we just want to develop the jazz canon and just focus, and we can’t focus on Bix Beiderbecke until we’ve focused on all these other people and that’s great. But you happened to mention, well what about Benny Goodman or what about Gil Evans and all, what about Bill Evans? Not that they should have whole concerts or whatever, but just to get his opinion. And he always like had some dismissive way of — like he’d say it’s just by coincidence, he’ll say it’s not racial. But just coincidentally if you bring up the name of any white — “we will never do Benny Goodman.” I mean I don’t know — we’ve got to finish up here, I don’t know when your next person is.

Yeah okay. But I mean it’s like an irony. See like you got me going now. But an irony. Now take Benny Goodman, who was really until recently known for this guy who broke the color barrier. He was the guy that hired Lionel Hampton and Teddy Wilson and he was, like with Benny Goodman died, that week I was doing a concert opposite Lionel Hampton and Lionel Hampton said, he got to the microphone and he said, “Benny Goodman was the Abraham Lincoln of jazz. If it wasn’t for him I wouldn’t be here doing as well as I am.” Now Benny Goodman was a strange personality and there’s a lot of people that didn’t like him and he was weird, there’s no question about that, I can tell you first-hand, although that isn’t the whole story. But for some reason I just see this thing happening, kind of like — I don’t know if it’s the Jewish thing, but it’s similar to like there was so much of a Jewish sympathy for the Civil Rights movement and so many, like Schwerner and Chaney, whatever, you know shot down there. And then there’s all this backlash against Jews. And I sort of find that, I mean I don’t know if it’s a Jewish thing or what it is, but for some reason, Benny Goodman, it’s been turned around from that he was helping black people, to he was exploiting them. He was buying these Fletcher Henderson arrangements for $25 and not giving him credit or whatever, and Fletcher’s band went out of business and Benny’s making all these hits, and it’s like instead of helping these black people it’s like he’s using them. And it’s like all these motives get really, just like there’s this lack of trust and lack of I think wanting to understand the situation. And I think there’s a general willingness for maybe younger black musicians to believe that it was worse for the older musicians than it was. Because although I think that Duke Ellington, when those guys traveled down south it was horrible. Louis Armstrong. I mean that’s on record. Those guys, it was miserable the things they had to deal with and nobody should have gone through that. But still, because this country, if something sells, people don’t care about black, white, whatever. Those

guys were able to get their music out. And artistically they were not stymied. Today I think it’s a little different because I just feel like certain people are just not being allowed to express themselves because of a racial thing that really it wasn’t. People want to think that it was that way back then with Duke and Louis Armstrong, but it wasn’t.
